Kit

Build a multiplayer game in a day

10 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓

Predicted combat presentation (1-2 hours)6. Enemies (1 hour)7. Loading levels from replicated state (1 hour)8. Runs end: match flow (1 hour)9. Quit and resume (30 minutes)9b. Carryable entities (30 minutes)9c. Host migration (30 minutes)9d. Shared-seed procgen (30 minutes)10. Connecting through Steam (1 hour + a friend)11. Headless acceptance tests12. Moving contested state to the simulation lane

This guided tour explains the co-op replication workflow by following the structure of examples/cavecrawl. Its snippets are excerpts, not a complete project. Start with the session quickstart if you want the smallest buildable example first; use the glossary for Kit terminology.

The tutorial builds an invited-peer game in which one player hosts a small co-op cave crawler. Cavecrawl is the complete reference implementation for the features introduced below.

Generated wrappers apply the declared authority, prediction, rejection, and presentation policies. The game implements target validation and mutation, accepted cross-entity consequences, authority steps, and presentation hooks.

0. The main game script#

Declare the session, communications, and Boot fields on the main game script. Cavecrawl calls this script CaveLobby:

Odin
CaveLobby :: struct {
	owner: gd.Node,
	ses:   ksess.Session,
	comms: kcomms.Comms,
	boot:  kboot.Boot,
	// ...your world: entity maps, UI handles, campaign state
}

Keep one session and one Boot on the script instead of in package globals. The session retains network identity, entities, and stats for rehosting and saved runs. Boot (kit/boot) holds the Godot-facing lobby, chat, scoreboard, stage/world containers, and transport wire. Its widgets are public fields that the game can restyle or ignore. Game-specific campaign state will need a separate save blob, described below.

1. Boot and lobby (15 minutes)#

In ready():

Odin
my_game_net_attach(self, kboot.Options{
	title    = "MY GAME",
	status   = "Host a cave, or join one at localhost",
	msg_kind = MSG_SESSION, // MSG_SESSION :: u8(0) — all kit/session traffic under one game byte
	env      = "MY", // MY_PORT/_NAME/_TOKEN identity + the MY_LATENCY shim
	methods  = {"on_host", "on_join", "on_start", "on_chat",
	            "on_packet", "on_peer_left", "on_net_up", "on_net_down"},
}, kboot.network_profile(.Friends_Coop))

The attach call creates the lobby title, status, player list, Host/Join/Start buttons, chat, scoreboard, and session transport wire. The boot: kboot.Boot field also generates four transport forwarders: on_packet/on_peer_left/on_net_up/on_net_down. They report transport changes to the session, which clears disconnected peers from the roster after Alt-F4, a crash, or connection loss. A hand-written method with the same name overrides a generated forwarder.

.Friends_Coop records that invited entity owners may author their streamed movement. Choose .Listen_Server_Action when clients send validated inputs to a player-hosted simulation, or .Dedicated_Competitive when that authority runs on trusted infrastructure. See Network profiles.

Implement the four UI methods for hosting, joining, starting, and chat. The Host handler calls kboot.boot_host(&self.boot, port, name); Join calls kboot.boot_join(&self.boot, addr, port, token, name). Each connection handler checks whether the action is allowed, calls Boot, and updates status text. Use an example game's net.odin as a starting point; its connection handlers take about 60 lines.

The join's token is the player identity (kboot.boot_token(&self.boot), persisted in user://my_token, overridable via MY_TOKEN so same-machine tests pick distinct seats). Presenting the same token later (after a crash, a quit, a resumed save) reclaims the same identity, stats, and entities. Persist it; never regenerate it. See session.

The attach call is generated from the shell's direct Boot, Session, and Comms fields. It also installs generated entity/message/migration wiring. In process(), one generated call pumps the wire, ticks the session, applies the stock reactions, and dispatches your event halves. A co-op authority step remains an explicit game decision because it commonly runs only while playing:

Odin
frame := my_game_net_frame(self, delta, now_s())

Generated dispatch runs synchronously inside my_game_net_frame, applying each hook's execution policy. For custom ordering, the component calls boot_attach/boot_pump/my_game_events and underlying wire_attach/wire_pump, session_tick/session_poll remain public. See boot, netgd, and session.

2. Your first replicated entity (30 minutes)#

An entity is a plain script struct with tagged fields:

Odin
//gd:extends Node2D
Chest :: struct {
	owner:  gd.Node2d,
	glyph:  gd.Label `gd:"onready=Glyph"`,
	net_id: knet.Net_Id,
	x, y:   f32 `gd:"replicate"`,
	slots:  [4]kitems.Slot `gd:"replicate"`,
}

Scriptgen generates serialization, dirty tracking, and a Command_Set. registry_insert writes the registered id into net_id. Add an entity= tag to the scene export to declare the scene's entity type and stable wire id:

Odin
// CaveLobby field: assign the scene in the Inspector and declare its entity type.
chest_scene: ^gd.Resource `gd:"entity=Chest:2"`,

The generated cave_lobby_net_attach installs cave_lobby_entities. On every peer, including the host, that factory instantiates scenes under boot.world, records each id and node, and frees the node on despawn. The tag also generates typed lookup and iteration procedures, so the game does not need a parallel entity map:

Odin
if chest, ok := chest_of(&self.boot, id); ok {
	inspect(chest)
}
for tracked in chest_all(&self.boot) {
	inspect(tracked.entity)
}

A custom shell may call the entity installer directly. Typed _spawned and _freed hooks remain for game-specific indexes or bookkeeping, not for recreating the registry.

On the host, call the generated chest_spawn helper. It returns a typed Chest pointer and id; initialize its fields, then announce the spawn:

Odin
chest, id := chest_spawn(&self.boot)
chest.x, chest.y = 300, 180
kboot.boot_spawn_send(&self.boot, id)

After replication starts, the per-tick delta walk sends changes to registered authority-written fields. Clients receive the current value; late joiners receive it in their snapshot.

3. Owner-streamed movement (30 minutes)#

Give players' avatars owner-streamed fields:

Odin
x, y: f32 `gd:"owner"`, // continuous owner fields interpolate by default

The entity owner writes these fields every frame. Kit sends their latest values over the unreliable channel; remote peers interpolate about 3 ticks in the past to absorb jitter and packet loss. Follow two rules:

  • Only the entity owner writes its owner-streamed position. For respawns, level changes, and knockbacks, the authority replicates state that tells the owner how to move its avatar. For example, restored hp can trigger the owner's respawn positioning.
  • Announce discontinuous position changes as teleports. On the frame of a level change, blink, or respawn, call the generated helper, such as spelunker_teleport(&self.boot, self.me). Otherwise remote peers interpolate across the position jump and show the avatar sliding across the map.

4. Commands and authority consequences (1 hour)#

A Kit command is a procedure on the entity it validates and mutates. Here a player requests items from a chest:

Odin
@(gd_command = knet.ACTION_ANY_SEAT_PREDICTED)
chest_take :: proc(self: ^Chest, slot: u8, count: u16, px, py: f32) -> (ok: bool, taken: kitems.Slot) {
	if !kinter.in_range({px, py, 0}, {self.x, self.y, 0}, REACH) {return false, {}}
	taken = kitems.take(self.slots[:], int(slot), count)
	return taken.count > 0, taken
}

The generated chest_take_cmd wrapper runs this command authoritatively on the host and predictively on clients. Returning false as the first result rejects the request and reverts its writes. An authority rejection also sends accepted state back to the predicting client. If two players request the last item, both can predict success. The host executes requests in arrival order, accepts the first, and rejects the second; that client then reverts its prediction.

A command may mutate only its target. To add the accepted loot to the player's inventory, implement its paired consequence, <verb>_then. Results after the applied boolean become payload arguments to that procedure, alongside the issuer and wire arguments. The consequence runs only on the authority, for both client-issued and host-issued commands. Client prediction never calls it:

Odin
@(gd_half)
chest_take_then :: proc(game: ^CaveLobby, self: ^Chest, by: knet.Player_Id, slot: u8, count: u16, px, py: f32, taken: kitems.Slot) {
	cave_credit(game, by, self, taken) // authority mutation replicated through deltas
}

Check stamina, cooldown, and life state before issuing a command. A locally refused prediction is still sent, so repeated unavailable actions create avoidable requests and rejection logs. See items and interact for the deterministic ops that are safe inside command procs.

5. Predicted combat presentation (1-2 hours)#

Cavecrawl's rocks.odin implements this projectile pattern in about 100 lines, using kit/fx for presentation:

  • The cast is a predicted command that checks its ability slot's cooldown and cost; see combat.
  • At cast time, the shooter starts a local kfx.Tracers visual. It needs no replicated projectile entity or network message before appearing.
  • The host simulates the projectile that applies damage and announces a kcombat.Fire through an app tag. Other peers start their visuals from the announcement, while the shooter skips the echo of its predicted cast.
  • On local visual contact, kcombat.php_note_hit reduces displayed hp through an overlay without changing the replicated field. An authoritative hp delta later consumes the overlay. If the host judges a miss, the overlay expires and displayed hp returns to its authoritative value.

Include the shooter's local origin in Fire. The host's owner-streamed copy of the shooter is delayed and would launch along a different path, especially while strafing. Bound the supplied origin on the host with kcombat.leash.

Test this behavior with injected latency: set Options.latency_env = "MY_LATENCY" and run under MY_LATENCY=120 (or call netgd.wire_set_latency(&self.boot.wire, 120) directly).

6. Enemies (1 hour)#

Use ai's helpers from a game-owned NPC update loop. A dweller is an ordinary entity owned by the host player. The host writes its streamed position and one replicated behavior byte; clients interpolate its motion and display that behavior. kai.Director and director_tick schedule waves from data. Private decision state lives in a host-side map keyed by net id and is rebuilt from the game's save blob on resume.

7. Loading levels from replicated state (1 hour)#

Store the current floor in a Level entity's depth: u8 field. When that value changes, each peer loads level_N.tscn locally. Static geometry stays in the scene files. The host reads Marker2D spawn points from its own scene and creates the dynamic session entities; .tres resources hold wave plans.

To descend, despawn the old floor's entities, increment depth, and build the next floor. New joiners and resumed saves receive the depth in the snapshot, so they can load the corresponding local scene through the same path.

8. Runs end: match flow (1 hour)#

Add won: u8 to the Level entity. Clearing the last floor sets it, and peers respond to the change by showing the scoreboard and status; the host's Start button offers another run. Restart clears won and rebuilds floor 1 within the same session. Seats, tokens, and cumulative stats remain in place while deltas carry the new run state.

Keep replicated state changes visible across a network tick. A byte that changes 1→0 within one tick produces no delta if its final value equals the stored comparison value. Use an explicit comms message or app tag for one-shot events that must be delivered.

If strangers can join, add moderation and admission policy deliberately. The tools are session_kick(player, ban), session_set_locked, and Session_Config.max_players, with netgd.wire_drop closing the kicked socket after the "you were kicked" message flushes. Returning identities pass lock and capacity checks when reclaiming their existing seats.

9. Quit and resume (30 minutes)#

Odin
// Save session state and the game-specific campaign blob.
ksave.save_write(&self.ses, &w, GAME_VERSION, my_campaign_blob)
// Restore session state and read the campaign blob.
blob, err := ksave.resume(&self.ses, name, path, GAME_VERSION)

The save snapshot carries session identity, stats, and entities using the same data used for backup hosting. The game adds a blob for private state such as the wave director and AI clocks. Friends rejoin the resumed run with their persisted tokens through the normal reconnect path. See save.

9b. Carryable entities (30 minutes)#

To carry an entity, give it owner-streamed position. A grab command's _then calls session_set_owner(ses, id, by). The game handles Ev_Owner_Changed and lets the carrier update its position each frame, such as relic.x = me.x + 10. Dropping assigns PLAYER_ID_INVALID, leaving the entity at its last position. Mounts, possession, and dragging bodies use the same ownership transfer and position update pattern.

For downed players, add a predicted revive command that checks range and sets hp = REVIVE_HP. The host tracks bleed-out time. When hp changes, the owner checks its value to distinguish revival in place from a bleed-out respawn. Cavecrawl's spelunker_revive demonstrates the pattern.

9c. Host migration (30 minutes)#

Periodic authority backups let another player resume hosting after the host disconnects. Declare four halves and pass their generated table to kboot.boot_migration in ready:

  • <game>_backup writes game-specific campaign bytes into each backup.
  • <game>_took_over reads them on the successor and restores private game state.
  • <game>_wiped clears non-entity pools after Kit removes tracked entities.
  • <game>_migrating updates status for each migration step.

Kit starts the handoff on Ev_Backup_Target. After dispatching session events, it either takes over or reconnects to the successor, bounds retries, and retains the timing state needed to manage the attempt. Act 4 of Cavecrawl's acceptance test kills the host with kill -9 and checks that handoff needs no manual input. See session.md for setup.

9d. Shared-seed procgen (30 minutes)#

Replicate a seed: u32 field on the level entity and generate decoration locally on each peer. Only the seed crosses the wire; generated scenery needs zero additional wire bytes. Cavecrawl's splitmix32 scatter uses integer math throughout so peers derive the same result. Floating-point generation can vary with FMA contraction, libm implementations, and fast-math flags; even a low-bit difference can change the generated cave. Cavecrawl's acceptance test compares checksums printed by both processes to verify matching decoration.

10. Connecting through Steam (1 hour + a friend)#

Use steamgd to connect the existing session through Steam lobby and peer APIs:

Odin
if steamgd.available() && steamgd.init(APP_ID) {
	steamgd.listen(self.owner, "on_lobby_created", "on_lobby_joined", "on_join_requested")
}
// host: create_lobby -> lobby_created -> host_peer -> invite_overlay
// guest: overlay "Join Game" -> join_requested -> join_lobby -> client_peer

Session_Wire continues receiving SceneMultiplayer signals through the selected MultiplayerPeer. Verify the Steam connection live with the Spacewar app id (480), a steam_appid.txt, and one friend.

11. Headless acceptance tests#

Cavecrawl's headless acceptance test starts two processes over ENet with 120ms injected latency. Its driver operates the scene tree and checks log lines from each peer (examples/cavecrawl/run.sh + cave_test.gd). Reproduce observed gameplay failures in a driver so its assertions can check the result on both peers. A test script can call the same @(gd_method) procedures used by gameplay input.

12. Moving contested state to the simulation lane#

This tutorial uses peer-owned movement, which is appropriate when the host trusts each owner to report its fast state. A duel, ranked game, or other contested design should derive movement from admitted input on the authority. Retag that state with predict, move its writes into @(gd_tick), and attach the simulation lane. Session identity, entities, commands, chat, and saves can remain on their existing lanes. Read Timelines to choose a model and kit/sim for the migration checklist.
